Barbara McClintock. The American geneticist who discovered transposable elements, or jumping genes, in maize. Her work revealed that the genome was dynamic and controllable, overturning the view of genes as static, unchanging units.

In the nineteen forties and nineteen fifties, McClintock discovered DNA sequences that could move from one location to another on chromosomes, causing visible mutations in corn kernels. She observed variegated corn kernels with spontaneous colour patterns and traced the instability through genetic analysis to mobile genetic elements she called Ac and Ds, standing for Activator and Dissociation. She realized that these transposable elements could regulate gene expression, turning genes on and off, a mechanism of genetic control that had been unknown before her work.

Her theories were initially met with scepticism from the scientific community. It was only during the molecular revolution of the nineteen sixties and seventies that her work was vindicated. Transposons were found in bacteria, fungi, and humans, confirming that she had discovered a fundamental feature of life itself. McClintock worked in isolation at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory for decades, conducting meticulous genetic experiments with maize over multiple generations.

She recognised that genetic variation and evolution depended not just on random mutation but on the genome's ability to reorganise itself. Thomas Hunt Morgan had established corn and Drosophila as model organisms before her, and McClintock used corn to reveal even deeper mechanisms. Later, Watson and Crick's DNA structure would explain at the molecular level what McClintock had observed genetically. In 1983, the year before her death, she won the Nobel Prize.
